explanations: luna: The verse asks how people disbelieve in God after being lifeless, brought to life, made to die, given life again, and returned to Him. This compact life-death-return sequence echoes the section's stages and its closing challenge about denial. | terra: The rebuke “How can you disbelieve?” is followed by lifelessness, life, death, renewed life, and return to God, an exact argumentative lifecycle.
terra: The Mount is raised above Israel at the covenant; this physical action confirms ṭūr's mountain sense against the section's secondary sound-play.
terra: The repeated covenant scene again has the Mount raised overhead, another concrete Qur'anic use of ṭūr as an object rather than a temporal stage.

luna: Among the signs named here is rain by which God gives life to earth after its death. This repeats the dead-ground scene the section notices in 22:5, placing it among signs for those who reason. | terra: Rain revives the earth after death and spreads creatures through it; this is a broad sign-scene corresponding to the revived field in 22:5.
terra: Two complete years of nursing provide a measured early-life interval after birth, complementing the womb stages emphasized in the section.
terra: Saul is increased in knowledge and body, pairing mature bodily amplitude with knowledge at the life-course summit before senile loss.

luna: The verse says God fashions people in the wombs as He wills. That directly extends the section's formed and unformed embryo detail and its account of bodily form taking shape. | terra: God forms people in wombs however He wills, directly locating the section's appearance of form within gestation.
terra: Zechariah says old age has reached him and his wife is barren; the closed reproductive stage becomes the setting for God's power to create new life.

luna: It says every soul tastes death and that recompense is completed on Resurrection Day. This links the end of the bodily course to the judgment and reward that remain beyond it. | terra: Every soul tastes death, but full recompense comes on Resurrection Day; bodily duration ends before reward is delivered.
terra: Orphans are tested until marriageable age and property is released when sound judgment appears, making maturation a threshold of capacity and responsibility.
terra: خُلِقَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ ضَعِيفًا states created human weakness; it bounds “best stature” by recalling the weakness from which strength rises and to which age returns.

terra: The section's dictionary sense of gh-y-r is change of form without change of self; Satan's command فَلَيُغَيِّرُنَّ خَلْقَ ٱللَّهِ gives a culpable, deliberate alteration of creation against involuntary aging.
terra: The Mount raised over the people for their covenant supplies the same distinct mountain sense on which the section's phonetic bridge depends.

luna: It says God created people from clay and appointed a term, then remarks that they still doubt. This connects the section's creation and measured lifespan to the very denial its closing question addresses. | terra: Creation from clay and the decree of a term are followed by human doubt, joining bodily origin, bounded lifetime, and denial in one ayah.
terra: Nightly taking and daytime raising continue until a named term, after which return and accounting come; the daily cycle models a bounded life and final return.
terra: Reaching full strength marks the point at which an orphan's property may be approached differently, giving maturity a concrete legal consequence.
terra: “We created you, then formed you” distinguishes origination from bestowed shape, the same distinction the section draws around completed form.
terra: كَمَا بَدَأَكُمْ تَعُودُونَ states that people return as God began them, directly linking first state and final return.
terra: Heavy clouds are driven to dead land, fruit emerges, and the ayah says the dead are brought out likewise.
terra: God increased the people in physical stature, a direct bodily-height parallel to the section's dictionary gloss of qiwām as completeness and length.
terra: A pregnancy passes from a light burden to heaviness before the parents ask for a sound child, supplying a distinct internal progression within the womb stage.
terra: After a sound child is granted in 7:189, the recipients associate partners with God; its own contribution is denial following the successful completion of gestation.

luna: The source section distinguishes the negating word غَيْرُ from its root's sense of alteration. This verse uses the root for a favor's condition changing when people change themselves; the connection to bodily aging is indirect, since its context is a community's moral state. | terra: God does not change a bestowed favor until a people change themselves, another volitional use of gh-y-r that bounds the section's involuntary bodily change.
terra: God begins creation and repeats it in order to reward believers who do right, directly joining first formation, return, and recompense.
terra: The parable of worldly life races from rain-fed abundance to sudden removal as though it had not flourished, another visible arc from formation to disappearance.

luna: The verse asks whether any of the partners can originate creation and then repeat it, and answers that God does so. It turns creation and return into a direct challenge about who has that power, like the section's final challenge after the life stages. | terra: The question asks which supposed partner can begin creation and then repeat it, and answers that God does both.
luna: The verse says God gives life and death and that to Him people return. This directly states the life-ending and return sequence developed by the section.
terra: An old woman with an elderly husband wonders at bearing a child, setting age's ordinary decline in fertility against divine creation.
terra: عَطَآءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ describes Paradise's gift as uncut, a direct semantic parallel to the section's reward that is not severed.
terra: When Joseph reaches full maturity, he receives judgment and knowledge; this supplies a concrete middle peak between newborn ignorance and old-age forgetting.

luna: The verse cites deniers asking whether they will be in a new creation after becoming dust, a direct reversal of the source section's dust-to-human beginning and a challenge to its return sequence.

luna: The verse says God knows what every female carries and what wombs diminish or increase, with all things measured by Him. It adds the womb's changing development and measure to the staged formation discussed in the section. | terra: God knows every pregnancy, what wombs diminish or increase, and every thing has its measure; this directly joins gestation to precise determination.

luna: The source section names غ ي ر and a dictionary sense of changing a thing's outward state while its essence remains. This verse uses the root for a people changing their condition; the sense is moral and social rather than bodily aging, but it offers a specific parallel of continuing identity through changed state. | terra: God does not يُغَيِّرُ a people's condition until they change what is within themselves; this moral change of state contrasts with bodily form changing through age.
terra: Flood foam vanishes while what benefits people remains on earth, a physical parable for the section's contrast between what is cut off and what endures.
terra: The garden promised to the mindful has lasting fruit and shade, giving concrete continuity to recompense beyond the changing body.
terra: God announces the creation of a mortal from clay before 15:29 describes proportioning him, so this ayah supplies that formed body's material beginning.
terra: God's command to prostrate comes only after the human has been proportioned and ensouled, making completed form a threshold.
terra: God creates the human from a drop, yet the formed human becomes an open adversary; the compressed beginning-to-denial arc closely matches the section's closing rebuke.

luna: The verse says rain gives life to earth after its death. It is a direct parallel to the revived dry ground that the section identifies as part of 22:5's proof. | terra: Rain revives earth after death as a sign for listeners, echoing the secondary field scene in 22:5 without itself explicitly naming human resurrection.

luna: The verse uses “يُرَدُّ” for those returned to the feeblest age, where knowledge fades after having been known. That directly supplies the old-age reading of the source section's root ر د د in 95:5. | terra: The ayah says some are يُرَدُّ إِلَىٰ أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ until knowledge is lost, directly identifying the section's return with senescence.

luna: People are brought from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then given hearing, sight, and hearts. This supplies the beginning-of-life knowledge state that contrasts specifically with 22:5 and 16:70, where old age may return a person to knowing nothing. | terra: Humans leave the womb knowing nothing and receive hearing, sight, and hearts; beside 16:70's old-age loss of knowledge, this makes life's cognitive arc return toward its beginning.

luna: The verse contrasts what people possess, which runs out, with what is with God, which remains, and promises the patient their reward. This concretely parallels the section's cut-off lifespan beside an “uninterrupted reward.” | terra: What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, followed by promised reward; this states the section's finite-life versus uncut-reward relation.
terra: The protection of an orphan's property lasts until full strength is reached, again treating maturity as a distinct threshold rather than an undivided lifespan.

luna: The verse quotes people asking whether they will be raised after becoming bones and fragments. That body-wearing image corresponds to the source section's dictionary branch of خ ل ق for something worn out. | terra: Bones and crumbled remains are invoked against becoming a new creation, turning the body's wearing away into a denial of the next stage.
terra: The command to become stone or iron intensifies the imagined barrier of bodily material rather than conceding that decay defeats return.

luna: In the 17:49–51 exchange, 17:49 raises the objection about bones and fragments; this verse asks “مَن يُعِيدُنَا,” who will restore the deniers after dissolution. Its own wording directly meets the section's return-root ر د د and its old-age/death arc. | terra: The answer “the One who originated you the first time” makes first formation overcome even the hardest imagined form.
terra: The children of Adam are honored and preferred over much creation, giving a dignity counterpart to the section's best human stature.
luna: This verse restates denial after becoming bones and fragments, asking whether people will be raised as a new creation. It makes the section's worn-body and return contrast explicit.

luna: Following the denial in 17:98, it argues that the Creator of the heavens and earth can create the like of them. This completes the first-creation/new-creation answer relevant to the section's staged making.

luna: The speaker says he does not think the Hour will come; 18:37 answers with his creation from dust, a drop, and full human form. This denial supplies the exact stance the section's staged-creation argument addresses.

luna: In response to a man's denial of the Hour, the companion recalls that God made him from dust, then a drop, then formed him as a man. That staged origin is used as a direct answer to denial, as in the section's final question. | terra: The believer asks whether his companion rejects the One who made him from dust, then a drop, then سَوَّىٰكَ رَجُلًا, a fully formed man.
terra: The parable of worldly life moves from rain-fed mingling growth to dry fragments scattered by wind, a natural image of formed life wearing out.
terra: Worldly adornments are set against enduring righteous deeds and their better reward, matching the section's reward beyond the body's decline.
terra: The two orphans are to reach full strength before extracting their treasure, making bodily maturity the appointed point of independent action.
terra: Zechariah's weakened bones and head blazing with gray hair make the bodily wearing of old age visible from within a single person.
terra: Extreme old age and a barren wife appear as bodily limits to be crossed by the promised child, illuminating senescence without making it ultimate.
terra: God's call to Moses from the right side of ٱلطُّورِ places the noun in the Sinai encounter, maintaining the semantic boundary from ṭawr, “stage.”
terra: The human asks incredulously whether he will be brought out alive after death, voicing the denial at the end of the section's timeline.
terra: The reply recalls that God created the human before he was anything, using the first beginning to answer the preceding resurrection doubt.
terra: Enduring righteous deeds are better in reward and return, supporting the section's claim that good action yields value beyond the changing life.
terra: Creation from earth, return into it, and emergence another time state the full outward-and-back arc that the section's stages imply.
terra: The appointment at the right side of ٱلطُّورِ again fixes the word as the Mount within the exodus story, not a creation stage.
terra: The flower of worldly life is a temporary test, while the Lord's provision is better and more lasting, another duration boundary around earthly flourishing.
terra: Every soul tastes death and is returned after testing; the relation to the section is specific to life's endpoint and moral outcome, but the bodily arc is unstated.
terra: God promises to repeat creation just as He began the first creation, making origination itself the measure of resurrection.

luna: This is the section's clearest full arc: the verse names the staged making of the embryo and then says some are “يُرَدُّ ... أَرْذَلَ ٱلْعُمُرِ,” returned to the feeblest age, losing knowledge; it then turns to dead earth stirred by rain as another sign of resurrection. The source section explicitly reads the named root ر د د as a return along life's course. | terra: This is the section's fullest stated parallel: dust, drop, clot, formed and unformed flesh, childhood, maturity, senescence, death, revived earth, and resurrection all occupy one evidentiary arc.

luna: This follows the staged creation and revived-earth scene in 22:5 and states their conclusion: God is the Truth and gives life to the dead. This is the verse's own contribution to the section's resurrection reading. | terra: This ayah draws the conclusion from 22:5's human and earth stages: God is the Truth, gives life to the dead, and has power over all things.

luna: Following 22:5–6, this verse says the Hour is coming and God will raise those in the graves. It supplies the judgment claim that the section asks how anyone could deny after seeing life's stages. | terra: The next ayah states the conclusion that the Hour will come and those in graves will be raised, completing the staged-creation argument cited by the section.
luna: The verse states that God gave people life, then causes death, then gives life again. This is a compact counterpart to the section's life-course ending in death and its question about return.

luna: The sequence begins with man's origin from clay, matching the first material stage named in the source section's account of 22:5. | terra: Human creation from an extract of clay begins the ordered stages that culminate in another creation at 23:14.

luna: The drop placed in a secure lodging continues the bodily-development sequence that the section traces from the womb onward. | terra: Placement as a drop in a secure lodging supplies the womb setting between clay-origin and the formed embryo.

luna: This verse gives the stages from a clinging form through a lump, bones, and flesh, then says “ثُمَّ أَنشَأْنَٰهُ خَلْقًا ءَاخَرَ” and praises Allah as “أَحْسَنُ ٱلْخَٰلِقِينَ.” The section explicitly joins this staged making and the phrase “best of creators” to its account of human form. | terra: The clot, morsel, bones, flesh, and emergence as another creation enact form becoming complete; أَحْسَنُ ٱلْخَٰلِقِينَ also joins creation to “best.”

luna: Following the formation sequence in 23:12–14, this verse says that people die afterward, matching the section's transition from life's stages to death cutting off its span. | terra: After the formative sequence of 23:12–14, this ayah marks the certain cutoff of those stages in death.

luna: After the death named in 23:15, this verse says people will be raised on Resurrection Day. That completes the creation-to-death-to-return sequence which the source section reads as a case for judgment. | terra: This ayah completes the preceding creation-and-death sequence with resurrection on the Day of Judgment, answering the section's final challenge to denial.
terra: The tree growing from طُورِ سَيْنَآءَ anchors ṭūr as Sinai and even joins the Mount to the olive, clarifying that the life-stage link is phonetic rather than the mountain's lexical meaning.

luna: The verse quotes the objection that people will be raised after dying and becoming dust and bones, a direct bodily-decay version of the denial challenged by the section. | terra: The objection that dust and bones cannot be raised treats the worn body's final state as an endpoint, precisely the denial challenged after the section's life course.
luna: This continues the objection in 23:82 by dismissing the promised resurrection as an old tale. It makes the denial of the return explicit in the same creation-and-death context.
terra: At death the person asks, “My Lord, return me,” making the cutoff of life the point at which a wished-for reversal becomes impossible.
terra: The requested return is for doing righteousness in the life left behind, but a barrier remains until resurrection; this sharply distinguishes finite opportunity from the later outcome.

luna: The verse asks whether people thought they were created without purpose and would not be returned. It gives the return-purpose question that the section's closing challenge raises after the life-course has been displayed.
terra: When children reach puberty, their rule of seeking permission changes to the adult rule, showing a bodily stage carrying a new social status.

luna: The verse describes rain used to revive a dead land and provide water for people and animals. The dead-land scene is a specific parallel to the closing sign in 22:5 that the section connects with resurrection. | terra: Water revives a dead land and gives drink to creatures; its relevance is the revived-land scene itself, while the ayah does not explicitly draw the resurrection inference.

luna: The verse asks who originates creation and repeats it, then also asks who brings water and revives the earth. It brings together both images developed in the section: human creation and land revived after death. | terra: Beginning creation and repeating it appear among the acts by which false partners are challenged, reinforcing the same creation-to-return inference.

luna: The verse says Moses reached maturity and full strength before being given judgment and knowledge. This is a specific instance of the adult-strength stage that the section places between early life and old age, though the local passage is Moses' biography. | terra: Moses receives judgment and knowledge upon reaching full strength and maturity, again marking the section's summit as a life stage with new capacity.
terra: Moses sees a fire from the side of ٱلطُّورِ; the concrete mountain scene distinguishes the source section's sound association from ayah meaning.
terra: The divine call at the side of ٱلطُّورِ identifies the same mountain setting and so guards the section's stated distinction between mountain and stage.
terra: Worldly provision and adornment are temporary, while what is with God is better and more lasting, restating the finite-versus-enduring boundary.

luna: It asks whether people have not seen how God originates creation and then repeats it. This is another explicit creation-to-re-creation formulation of the inference the section draws from human stages. | terra: The question asks whether people see how God begins creation and then repeats it, matching the section's appeal to visible creation as evidence.
terra: Observation of how creation began leads explicitly to ٱلنَّشْأَةَ ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةَ, completing the first-life-to-next-life inference.

luna: The verse says every soul will taste death and then be returned to God, a concise version of the section's life-ending and onward-return sequence. | terra: Every soul tastes death and is then returned to God; this plausibly compresses the cutoff and return, though it does not display the intervening stages.

luna: The verse asks who sends rain and revives the earth after its death; the answer given is Allah. Its own contribution is the recognition of the same dead-land revival scene the section reads as evidence beyond ordinary decline. | terra: Rain revives earth after its death, another direct recurrence of the secondary field scene that 22:5 uses as evidence.

luna: The verse calls worldly life passing amusement and says the true life is the Hereafter. It makes explicit the finite-life/lasting-beyond-it contrast that the section develops through death and an uncut reward. | terra: The worldly life is play and diversion while the Hereafter is the true life, a boundary between passing stages and lasting existence.
terra: God begins creation, repeats it, and then people return to Him, a concise statement of the full trajectory beyond bodily decline.
terra: Bringing living from dead, dead from living, and reviving earth culminate in the promise that humans will be brought out in the same way.
terra: Creation from dust followed by people spreading as full humans telescopes the rise from material beginning to mature embodied life.
terra: Rain gives life to earth after its death as a sign for people who reason, repeating the visible revival stage without explicitly naming human resurrection in this ayah.

luna: The verse says God originates creation and then repeats it, and that this is easy for Him. It gives a direct repeated-creation counterpart to the section's staged creation and return. | terra: God begins creation and repeats it, a repeated direct formulation of the inference from first formation to later origination.
terra: God creates, provides, causes death, and gives life; the four acts place the finite human span inside divine origination and renewal.

luna: The verse asks the reader to see how God gives life to earth after its death and then says He gives life to the dead. It develops the same rain-revived-earth proof that the section notices in 22:5. | terra: The command to observe earth revived after death ends by affirming that the same One revives the dead, repeating the section's evidentiary analogy.

luna: The verse traces people from weakness to strength and back to weakness and gray hair, matching the section's rising and declining bodily course. | terra: Weakness, strength, then weakness and gray hair give the same temporal contour as best bodily completion followed by reversal.

luna: The verse describes a mother carrying a child through weakness upon weakness and weaning him over two years. It supplies gestation and infancy as concrete stages within the section's wider life-course image. | terra: The mother bears the child in weakness upon weakness and weans it in two years, adding measured infancy and maternal bodily change to the lifetime image.
terra: Knowledge of what is in wombs and where a soul will die places hidden human origin and hidden endpoint within one ayah.

luna: It says God began man's creation from clay, another statement of the material beginning that the section includes in its account of human stages. | terra: أَحْسَنَ كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقَهُۥ joins “best” with creation and begins human creation from clay, closely echoing best created form.

luna: It says human descendants were made from an extract of fluid, adding the reproductive beginning to the clay origin in 32:7 and to the section's staged development. | terra: The descendant is then made from an extract of lowly fluid, supplying the next human stage in the local sequence.

luna: It says God fashioned the human and gave hearing, sight, and hearts, a specific completion of bodily formation that complements the section's reading of taqwīm as achieved form. | terra: ثُمَّ سَوَّىٰهُ describes the human as proportioned before receiving faculties, matching form's completion at the section's summit.

luna: The verse records the objection that people will be recreated after being lost in the earth. This is the same denial of return from a body's dissolution that the section's creation-to-death arc puts in question. | terra: After 32:7–9 recount creation and proportioning, the objection to being a new creation when lost in earth enacts the very denial the section finds unreasonable.
luna: It answers the objection in 32:10 by naming the Angel of Death and saying people will be returned to their Lord, completing the body's death-to-return sequence.

luna: The deniers say that after bodies have disintegrated in the earth, they will be in a new creation. This gives a direct bodily-decay counterpart to the source section's named worn-out sense of خ ل ق and its question about return.
terra: Rain revives a dead land and the ayah concludes كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلنُّشُورُ, making seasonal revival a model of human rising.

luna: The verse moves from dust to a drop, then speaks of conception, birth, maturity, and a lifespan being shortened or extended. It makes life's bodily stages and measured duration explicit. | terra: Dust, drop, pairing, womb knowledge, long life, and life shortened are all held in a record, directly joining formation to measured lifespan.
terra: The condemned are reminded that they were given a life long enough to take warning, making completed lifespan the evidence that precedes judgment.

luna: The verse names dead earth revived to produce grain as a sign. This is a specific parallel to the rain-stirred land at the end of 22:5 in the section's resurrection argument. | terra: A dead earth revived to produce grain offers the same visible movement from lifelessness to productive life, though resurrection is supplied by the surrounding argument.

luna: It says that one given long life is “نُنَكِّسْهُ فِى ٱلْخَلْقِ,” turned back in creation. This is the section's aging reversal after the body's best form; it states the reversal directly. | terra: نُنَكِّسْهُ فِى ٱلْخَلْقِ makes long life an inversion within creation, the section's precise reading of being returned downward in old age.
terra: A human created from a drop becomes an open disputant; the sudden span from origin to denial mirrors the section's rebuke after displaying a lifetime.

luna: The verse describes the challenge about rotten bones (“وَهِىَ رَمِيمٌ”) and says the challenger forgot his own creation (“خَلْقَهُ”). The source section names خ ل ق's dictionary branch for things becoming worn; this verse makes bodily decay and forgotten creation the concrete issue. | terra: The denier forgets his own creation and asks who can revive decayed bones, concretizing the section's point that created form wears away.

luna: This answers the rotten-bones question in 36:78 by saying the One who created them the first time will give them life. It completes the decay-and-return connection in the preceding verse. | terra: The answer is that the One who originated the bones the first time will revive them, turning first creation into evidence for return.
terra: The production of fire from a green tree supplies a concrete transformation immediately after the answer about reviving decayed bones.
terra: The Creator of heavens and earth is declared able to create the like of humans, continuing the answer to the objection from bodily decay.
terra: In a resurrection dispute, the addressees are reminded that God created them from sticky clay, using their first material origin to test the claim that renewed creation is difficult.

luna: The verse asks whether people will be raised after death as dust and bones, connecting bodily decay to the return that follows the section's lifespan arc. | terra: The question whether dead dust and bones can be raised repeats the boundary that bodily decay seems to impose but resurrection crosses.
terra: Paradisal provision is described as having no exhaustion, a concrete semantic parallel to reward that is not cut off.
terra: The announced creation of a human from clay precedes the proportioning in 38:72 and thus contributes the initial material stage of the same sequence.
terra: As in 15:29, proportioning the human precedes the breathed spirit and angelic prostration, linking completion of form with elevated status.

luna: The phrase “خَلْقًا مِّنۢ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ” describes creation after creation in the wombs, matching the section's staged development and its discussion of the خ ل ق root. | terra: خَلْقًا مِّنۢ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ in three womb-darknesses supplies the section's exact creation-after-creation formulation.
terra: Rain-fed plants vary in color, wither, yellow, and become debris; their visible stages parallel bodily rise and deterioration.
terra: God takes souls at death and during sleep, retains the one decreed to die, and releases the other until a named term, making duration and its cutoff explicit.
terra: Those judged acknowledge two deaths and two lives, retrospectively recognizing that earthly death was one transition rather than the last state.
terra: Worldly life is temporary enjoyment while the Hereafter is the lasting home, directly setting the finite span against what endures after it.

luna: It says God formed people and made their forms good, a direct parallel to the section's account of the human body's completed form. | terra: صَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ directly states that God formed people and made their forms beautiful, clarifying “best stature” as completed embodiment.

luna: The verse lays out the course from dust and a drop to birth, maturity, old age, and an appointed term, giving a fuller lifespan sequence alongside the section's account. | terra: The ayah lays out dust, drop, clot, childhood, full strength, old age, earlier death, and an appointed term, matching the section's entire ascent and decline.

luna: After 40:67 traces birth, maturity, old age, and a term, this verse says God gives life and causes death and that His command brings things into being. Its own contribution is to state the divine life-and-death power behind that lifespan.

luna: It gives the same promise of “أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ” to those who believe and do good, directly echoing the reward phrase the section sets against death. | terra: Believers who do good receive أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, the section's exact claim that reward continues when bodily stages end.

luna: The verse pairs a humbled earth stirred by rain with God's power to give life to the dead. This is a close counterpart to the dead ground revived at the end of 22:5, which the section treats as resurrection evidence. | terra: The humbled earth trembles and swells with water, and its reviver is declared able to revive the dead; this is the exact secondary earth-scene noted from 22:5.

luna: The verse contrasts the enjoyment of worldly life with what is better and more lasting with God. It makes explicit the passing-life/lasting-reward distinction that the section draws from death and “أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ.” | terra: Worldly goods are temporary enjoyment, whereas what is with God is better and more lasting for believers, aligning duration with faith.

luna: It says that God revives a dead land with measured rain and immediately adds, “كَذَٰلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ,” likewise you will be brought forth. That makes explicit the earth-to-resurrection link noted in the section's reading of 22:5. | terra: Measured rain revives a dead land and كَذَٰلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ explicitly maps that scene onto human emergence.

luna: The verse lists rain from heaven and the earth revived after its death among God's signs. This repeats the precise land-revival image the section identifies at the end of 22:5. | terra: Provision descends from the sky and revives earth after death within a list of signs, preserving the same secondary natural parallel.

luna: The verse quotes people who say only worldly life exists, that they die and live, and that time destroys them. This is the explicit denial of any return against which the section's life stages and final question are set.
luna: The verse says God gives life, causes death, and gathers people for the Day of Resurrection. It directly answers the mortal course in the section with the return that follows it.

luna: It traces gestation and nursing to maturity and the age of forty, making pregnancy, growth, and adulthood part of a human lifespan sequence. | terra: Gestation and weaning, attainment of full strength, and the age of forty make a measured human timeline whose mature response is gratitude and good action.
terra: Against the grateful mature person of 46:15, this grown child scoffs at the promise of being brought out after death, showing denial as one possible outcome of reaching maturity.

luna: This verse begins the rain-to-growth passage completed in 50:11: water grows gardens and grain, while 50:11 supplies the explicit dead-land-to-emergence link. Its own rain-grown land scene parallels the revived ground the section notes in 22:5.

luna: After rain-grown gardens and grain in 50:9–10, this verse calls the revival of dead land provision and says, “كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلْخُرُوجُ,” thus is the emergence. It completes the same soil-to-resurrection scene mentioned in the section. | terra: Rain gives life to a dead land and كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلْخُرُوجُ identifies it with resurrection, matching the secondary proof inside 22:5.

luna: The verse asks whether God was wearied by the first creation and says the deniers are confused about a new creation. The contrast between the completed first making and denied return directly answers the section's challenge after life's stages. | terra: ٱلْخَلْقِ ٱلْأَوَّلِ is set against doubt about خَلْقٍۢ جَدِيدٍۢ, making first creation the direct proof of renewed creation.

luna: The section identifies 95:2's طُور as the mountain in the oath and links its sound to the source-section dictionary form ṭawr, “stage.” 52:1 again swears by “ٱلطُّورِ”; it preserves the mountain-oath half of that image, though its local argument is not about bodily stages. | terra: وَٱلطُّورِ is another oath by the Mount; it confirms that Qur'anic ṭūr names the mountain even though the section deliberately hears the homophonous “stage.”

luna: The source section names م ن ن in the phrase for an uncut reward and also gives “al-manūn” as a death that cuts life's span. This verse says opponents await “رَيْبَ ٱلْمَنُونِ” for the Prophet; the phrase can mean a turn of fate or time's calamity, including death, so its connection to the section's death sense is plausible but lexically less certain. | terra: The section's dictionary noun al-manūn names death because it cuts duration; رَيْبَ ٱلْمَنُونِ is precisely the death or fatal turn the opponents await.
terra: God knows people when He brings them from earth and while they are embryos in their mothers' wombs, spanning material origin and concealed formation.
terra: God creates the male and female pair before 53:46 identifies the emitted drop, so this ayah contributes differentiation within completed human form.

luna: The verse names creation from an emitted drop, a repeated Qur'anic formulation of the early bodily stage that the section traces through the womb. | terra: Creation from an emitted drop provides the bodily beginning immediately before the passage asserts the later origination.
terra: وَأَنَّ عَلَيْهِ ٱلنَّشْأَةَ ٱلْأُخْرَىٰ makes the second origination belong to the same Creator who produced the drop-stage.
terra: Every being on earth is passing away, universalizing the section's claim that created form wears out.
terra: The enduring face of the majestic Lord remains when created beings pass, sharpening the boundary between finite creation and what does not end.
terra: Paradise fruit is neither cut off nor withheld, giving material shape to the section's unsevered recompense.

luna: The verse quotes deniers asking whether they will be raised after becoming dust and bones, directly matching the section's passage from formed life to death and disputed return. | terra: The same dust-and-bones objection appears inside a passage already reasoning from human creation and measured death.

luna: The verse says God created people, setting up the passage's challenge about who creates human life that the section treats as a visible sequence of stages. | terra: نَحْنُ خَلَقْنَٰكُمْ فَلَوْلَا تُصَدِّقُونَ couples human creation with a rebuke for failing to affirm, closely matching the section's final stance.

luna: It asks the reader to consider the fluid people emit, naming a concrete reproductive beginning that corresponds to the section's drop-to-embryo progression. | terra: The question “Have you considered what you emit?” introduces the seed whose Creator is identified in 56:59, so its own contribution is the visible first material stage.

luna: After 56:58 asks about emitted fluid, this verse asks whether people create it or God is its Creator. Its own contribution is to make human formation an argument about the Creator, like the section's use of the stages before its challenge to denial. | terra: The question whether humans create the emitted seed or God does identifies the true agent of the first bodily stage.

luna: The verse says God has ordained death among people and cannot be thwarted, directly matching the section's claim that death cuts off a human lifespan. | terra: نَحْنُ قَدَّرْنَا بَيْنَكُمُ ٱلْمَوْتَ makes death a measured terminus within the creation sequence.

luna: It continues that death statement by saying God can replace people and bring them forth in a form they do not know. This makes the section's changing bodily form and return part of a larger creation argument. | terra: Replacing human likenesses and originating people in an unknown form extends the section's change of form beyond senescence.

luna: Following death and transformation in 56:60–61, the verse recalls the first creation and asks why people do not take heed. It explicitly ties the known life-course to God's power to create anew. | terra: Knowledge of the first origination is made the reason to remember, exactly the section's argument from life's seen stages to what follows.

luna: It tells listeners that God gives life to earth after its death, another direct formulation of the land-revival image developed through 22:5. | terra: God's revival of earth after death is offered as a clarified sign for understanding, supporting the dry-earth proof explicitly noticed in the section.
terra: Worldly life and a plant both pass through attraction, growth, yellowing, and debris, while the ayah sets that wearing cycle against the Hereafter.
terra: The death people flee will meet them and they will then be returned for disclosure of their deeds, joining life's cutoff to judgment.
terra: Before death arrives, the dying person wishes for a brief delay in order to give and become righteous; the ayah connects life's cutoff to deeds that would affect the lasting outcome.
terra: No soul is delayed once its appointed term arrives, specifying the irreversible cutoff implied by the section's al-manūn gloss.

luna: The verse says God created and formed people and made their forms good (“وَصَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ”), directly echoing the section's claim that the human form reaches its best completion. | terra: صَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ joins bestowed human form, its excellence, and final return in one ayah.

luna: The verse reports the claim that the dead will not be raised and answers that they certainly will. That is the precise denial of the return the section challenges after laying out human creation and death.
terra: Death and life are created as a test of who is best in deed, joining the cut lifespan to the moral outcome that survives it.

luna: The verse promises the Prophet “لَأَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ,” using the same uncut-reward wording that the section contrasts with the span of mortal life. | terra: أَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ repeats the uncut reward formula; its singular addressee shows the phrase's promise beyond the general believer formula.
terra: Nuh asks why his people do not accord God due majesty; 71:14 supplies their staged creation as the reason, paralleling the section's rebuke after the stages are shown.

luna: The source section links the mountain-name ṭūr in 95:2 with its dictionary form ṭawr, “stage,” by sound rather than by the oath's meaning. Noah's “أَطْوَارًا” uses that root in the actual sense of humans being made in stages. | terra: The section hears ṭawr, “stage,” behind ṭūr; this ayah directly says God created people أَطْوَارًا, in successive stages.
terra: A Day that makes children gray-haired catastrophically compresses the ordinary childhood-to-grayness trajectory and locates that reversal at Judgment.
terra: The question whether the human expects to be left without purpose opens a sequence that answers through his bodily origin and resurrection.

luna: The verse asks whether man was not a drop of emitted fluid, a first bodily stage that begins the same surah's creation-to-resurrection argument. | terra: The ayah places the human at the emitted-drop stage, opening the same formation sequence that the section follows toward complete stature.

luna: It moves from the drop to a clinging form and says God created and proportioned him, directly paralleling the section's developmental stages and completed bodily form. | terra: The clot is then خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ, created and proportioned, directly expressing the section's completion of form.

luna: The verse continues the formation sequence by making the two sexes, another concrete stage in the creation argument. | terra: The male and female are made from the preceding embryonic stages, marking differentiation within completed human formation.

luna: After the drop, clinging form, and formation in 75:37–39, the verse asks whether that Creator can give life to the dead. Its own contribution is the explicit resurrection conclusion the section draws after displaying life's stages. | terra: After the embryonic sequence, the question whether its Maker can revive the dead reproduces the section's move from visible life stages to Judgment.
terra: The ayah reaches behind formed life to a stretch of time when the human was not yet a thing mentioned, marking the zero point of the section's stages.

luna: The verse says man was created from a mixed drop to be tested and given hearing and sight, adding a concrete beginning-of-life stage to the section's human-development arc. | terra: Creation from a mixed drop proceeds to hearing and sight for a test, showing faculties emerging from an unformed beginning.

luna: It asks whether people were not created from a lowly fluid, directly naming the initial bodily material in the section's staged account. | terra: The rhetorical أَلَمْ نَخْلُقكُّم مِّن مَّآءٍۢ مَّهِينٍۢ begins an argument from the reader's own earliest stage.

luna: The verse says that fluid was placed in a secure lodging, supplying a specific womb detail alongside the section's formed and unformed stages. | terra: The lowly fluid is placed in a secure womb, locating the first stage before bodily form appears.

luna: After 77:20–21 names the fluid and its lodging, this verse says it remains there until a known term. Its contribution is the measured duration of gestation that joins the section's developmental stages to time. | terra: إِلَىٰ قَدَرٍۢ مَّعْلُومٍۢ gives gestation a known measure and endpoint, matching the section's staged timeline.

luna: Following the fluid, lodging, and term in 77:20–22, this verse says God measured it. It makes the measured ordering of bodily development explicit. | terra: فَقَدَرْنَا declares divine measuring after the womb sequence and turns it into an appeal to recognize the One who forms.
terra: The warning to deniers immediately after 77:20–23 parallels the section's question of how Judgment can still be denied after human formation is displayed.
terra: The deniers ask whether they will be مَرْدُودُونَ to the former state; the section's downward return in age is set beside the denied return after death.

luna: The verse voices the objection that decayed bones could not be restored, directly connecting bodily wearing and the denied return to the section's lifecourse. | terra: Their objection points to decayed bones, making worn created matter the boundary they wrongly treat as preventing restoration.
luna: This continues 79:11 by calling such restoration a losing return, explicitly naming the return that the section's final question says remains to be denied.
terra: A single blast answers the preceding question about return from decayed bones; its own contribution is the effortless event that initiates restoration.
terra: After that blast, the dead are suddenly on the open surface, supplying the actual restored state denied in 79:10–11.
terra: The rebuke of human ingratitude begins the birth-to-resurrection sequence, giving the section's final challenge a close rhetorical counterpart.
terra: The question “From what did He create him?” directs attention to the bodily beginning before 80:19 supplies the drop and measure.

luna: The verse says man was created from a drop and proportioned. It joins the section's initial developmental material to its claim that human form is brought to completion; the source section names خ ل ق for that making. | terra: مِن نُّطْفَةٍ خَلَقَهُۥ فَقَدَّرَهُۥ joins creation from a drop to exact determination, a concise parallel to formation and bodily measure.
terra: After creation and measuring, ثُمَّ ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُۥ places the lived course between formation and death.
terra: Within the ordered sequence begun at 80:18, this ayah makes death and burial the end of the earthly span.
terra: ثُمَّ إِذَا شَآءَ أَنشَرَهُۥ carries the same ordered sequence beyond death into resurrection.
terra: The question what deluded the human concerning his generous Lord opens the formation-to-denial sequence and parallels the section's closing interrogation.

luna: The verse says God created, proportioned, and balanced the human being (“خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ”), a close parallel to the section's reading of taqwīm as completed bodily form. | terra: خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ names creation, proportioning, and bodily adjustment together, directly paralleling completed form and best stature.

luna: It completes the preceding formation statement by saying God assembled man in whatever form He willed, giving the section's account of formed bodily shape a direct counterpart. | terra: فِىٓ أَىِّ صُورَةٍۢ مَّا شَآءَ رَكَّبَكَ makes the human form a divinely composed configuration, clarifying the section's concern with changing form.
terra: After 82:7–8 describe bodily formation, كَلَّا بَلْ تُكَذِّبُونَ بِٱلدِّينِ makes denial of Judgment the same startling response challenged in 95:7.
terra: The human is laboring onward to the Lord and will meet Him, compressing an earthly course and its final encounter into one address.
terra: The section reads human life as successive states; لَتَرْكَبُنَّ طَبَقًا عَن طَبَقٍ directly presents passage from stage to stage.
terra: Immediately after “stage after stage,” the question why they do not believe supplies the same astonished stance as 95:7.
terra: بَلِ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ يُكَذِّبُونَ names denial after the sequence of stages, preparing the identical exception and reward in 84:25.
terra: The painful punishment announced after stage-followed-by-denial stands opposite the unceasing reward in 84:25, completing that passage's two outcomes.

luna: The verse promises believers and doers of good an “أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ,” the same phrase as 95:6 and the section's contrast between a life cut short and an uncut reward. | terra: After 84:19's successive states and the intervening denial, this ayah repeats the section's exact outcome for believers who do good: أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ.
terra: إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ يُبْدِئُ وَيُعِيدُ compresses beginning and repetition into a single divine action pair.
terra: The command that the human look at what he was created from adopts the section's method of making bodily origin an argument.

luna: It names man as created from a gushing fluid, a bodily origin stage that begins this passage's argument about return. | terra: Creation from gushing fluid states the earliest material stage in that argument.

luna: The verse specifies where that fluid emerges, continuing the creation detail that the section's staged-development image calls to mind. | terra: The fluid's bodily source continues 86:5–6's origin scene; its anatomical formulation is relevant only as part of that formation-to-return argument, not as a separate life stage.

luna: After the account of human origin in 86:5–7, it says God is surely able to return man. This is the passage's explicit creation-to-return inference. | terra: After identifying human origin, the ayah declares God able to return him, moving from first formation to return.
terra: ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ compresses creation and proportioning into the same pairing used in the detailed human-stage passages.
terra: Divine measuring and guidance follow creation and proportioning in 87:2, giving ordered fitness to the formed creature.
terra: God brings out pasture, beginning a compact created-life sequence that ends in withered matter in the next ayah.
terra: The pasture is made dark stubble, an elemental analogue for created form passing from fullness to worn remains.

luna: The verse says people prefer worldly life. Against the source section's mortal course ending in death, this stance gives a concrete reason someone might neglect the lasting reward it describes. | terra: Preferring the nearer life fixes desire on the passing side of the section's finite-life and enduring-reward boundary.

luna: It says the Hereafter is better and more lasting, a direct contrast to the mortal lifespan beside the section's uncut reward. | terra: The Hereafter is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, supplying the enduring side that outlasts bodily stages.
terra: The human is created in toil; this qualifies bodily excellence by naming the arduous condition through which the life's stages pass.

luna: It says man was created from a clinging clot, a specific womb stage also named in the source section's staged account; the source section's root خ ل ق is used here for making. | terra: خَلَقَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ names the clot-stage alone, a concise occurrence of the formative sequence developed at length elsewhere.
terra: عَلَّمَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ marks knowledge gained after initial ignorance, the reverse edge of the section's senile “knows nothing after knowledge.”
terra: The oath by time directly frames the chronological reading that the section develops from the human body's successive states.
terra: After the oath by time, the human is declared to be in loss, giving a compressed counterpart to created strength passing into decline.
terra: The exception for faith and righteous deeds matches 95:6 and identifies what escapes the loss announced over time.
